This message comes from Capital One with the Capital One Saver card.

Capital One.
What's in your wallet?
Terms apply.
Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump is delivering remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting
Pool and PR's Tamara Keith reports this is where he will make his final
pitch to voters for the midterms.
The Reflecting Pool was the backdrop for Martin Luther King's "I Have
a Dream" speech in 1963, but this year it was at the heart of controversy
as President Trump boasted about its restoration before falsely blaming
vandalism for what the Justice Department later admitted was actually
a rushed and botched job.
Repairs are now completed.
A White House official tells NPR Trump's remarks will focus on "restoring
our great capital" and also a closing message before the midterms about
what the administration and Republicans in Congress accomplished
over the past two years.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
The advertising tracking firm Ad Impact says that at more than $573
million, the Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Tallarico is
the most expensive non-presidential race on record.
Polls show the close contest between Paxton, the Republican state AG
and Tallarico, a state lawmaker, has become a key indicator of voter
frustration with President Trump's policies and his congressional allies.
Nicole Rages is a special education teacher outside an Austin polling center.
She's telling voters it's time to get out their vote.
Voting is power.
And I'll tell you, I'll say what I tell, there are people in my life who, you
know, I'm close to that refuse to vote.
And I'll tell you what I tell them is that I don't think you have a right
to complain if you haven't done everything you could to make a change.
That interview, courtesy of Blaise Ganey with member station KUT.
Well, federal investigators are trying to determine what caused a small plane
from Texas to the Bahamas to suddenly crash in South Florida yesterday.
Video shows the aircraft crashing to the ground in a Palm Beach area and
bursting into flames.
Authorities say all nine people on board were killed.
No one on the ground was injured.
For the second time in less than a month, dozens of supermarkets across
Europe have been hacked.
Here's Rebecca Rossman.
Supermarkets in at least six European countries were affected, including
Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and the Netherlands.
Several stores reported temperatures inside their fridges and freezers
reaching 122 degrees Fahrenheit.
One supermarket chain in Belgium said it lost over $100,000 worth of produce.
It's unclear who is behind the latest attacks, which come just weeks
after similar attacks hit more than 400 supermarkets across France.
France's national cybersecurity agency says hackers took control of
refrigeration controllers supplied by a Danish company, costing
supermarkets tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food.
Rebecca Rossman, NPR News, Paris.
This is NPR News.
The Education Department has released new data that show a growing number
of colleges where student loan borrowers are struggling to repay their
loans, more from NPR's Corey Turner.
The data show what share of a college's student loan borrowers since
2020 are late or in default.
At one end, you'll find lots of top notch schools with very low nonpayment
rates, UNC Chapel Hill, University of Michigan, Princeton, all have
nonpayment rates around 4% of students.
But at the opposite end, the number of colleges where 40% or more of
students are in nonpayment is high and rising.
Most of these are private for-profit schools that specialize in short term
training for jobs like hair stylist and HVAC technician.
And there the data show a nonpayment crisis at more than a thousand
schools, at least a third of borrowers are not repaying their loans.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
The Department of Justice has asked the U.S.
Supreme Court to wade into its feud with California over the state's
voter rolls after a federal district judge and a divided Ninth Circuit
Court of Appeals panel rejected the DOJ's request to order California
to set aside and stop processing the ballots of thousands of people.
The DOJ filed a notice that it plans to appeal to the high court.
It remains to be seen whether the Supreme Court will agree to intervene
and whether it would weigh in before election day if it does.
The DOJ says it has identified 20,000 likely non-citizens on California's
voter roll whose ballots should not be counted until their citizenship can be verified.
This is NPR News.
